BasePK: 2471607

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct this question to the Minister of Industry. Since only 1 per cent of highway accidents can be attributed to defective automobiles, will the minister give some indication as to what progress is being made by way of legislation to reduce the heavy toll being suffered through other causes over which the government does have jurisdiction? On January 25 I put a similar question to the Prime Minister, at which time he promised a statement would be made by the minister responsible.

BasePK: 2471781

Speech:
Perhaps the minister will keep himself calm and in his general good humour while I develop my argument.
Provincial governments have no access to indirect fields of taxation. While they have access to income and corporation tax fields it is virtually impossible to go beyond or very far beyond the amount which is agreed upon under tax sharing arrangements; otherwise there would be double taxation. This leaves provincial governments with several choices.
Provincial governments must acquire their revenue from licences and royalties on the development of raw materials and resources, through direct retail sales taxes or through per capita taxes, which is the most regressive of all forms of taxation. Finally, they can raise taxes through taxation of property, but in practically all provinces this has been turned over to the municipalities as their exclusive field. What the provincial governments have to do is decide within the sources they have which is the least onerous and which is likely to be the most equitable form of taxation.
When the province of Saskatchewan had to raise money for hospital care, and you will remember that Saskatchewan instituted its hospitalization plan 11 years before such plans became general across Canada and financed the entire burden itself, it collected the money in three ways, by a small per capita tax which every family paid, by a sales tax and from general revenue.
When medicare came in the same thing had to be done. Some of the money had to be raised by sales tax, some by a small per capita tax, and some of it came out of general revenue. That does not mean that a sales tax is the most equitable form of raising revenue, but it is more equitable than taxing property and it is more equitable than a per capita tax on every family. Certainly it is not by any stretch of the imagination a tax which is best calculated to obtain revenue on the basis of an individual's ability to pay.

BasePK: 2471787

Speech:
No. The minister knows, because he is an economist, the difference between a retail tax and a tax at the manufacturer's level. The tax in Saskatchewan, and in all other provinces now but one, is on the retail price that people pay. If you buy a $1 article you know you will pay an additional 5 cents. Even the minister knows that. That is very different from imposing 12 per cent on the manufacturer's price. Heaven only knows what happens to the retail price then because when you buy an article in the store you do not know how much of the price you pay is federal sales tax and how much you are actually paying for the commodity. The fact is that the minister had to raise $290 million. He is raising the minor part of it on the basis of ability to pay, and well o\ er 50 per cent of it from the people who can least afford to pay it, the people who have to buy ordinary goods in the stores.
The minister says that we in this party are always talking about the things we would like to see done. He made an inventory, and I wish to thank him for it, of the things we have been advocating. He says these would cost some $900 million.

BasePK: 2471871

Speech:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the measure before the house is to add a further three year period during which loans made by chartered banks under this act may be guaranteed by the government and to extend the scope of the act in order to make its benefits available to a large number of small businesses.
I am sure hon. members will recall that this act was passed in 1961 to empower the government to guarantee loans made by chartered banks to small businesses engaged in manufacturing, trade or services for purchasing equipment and improving or enlarging the premises in which they operate. An amendment in 1962 extended the purposes for which loans may be made to include the purchase or building of premises, where existing premises cease to be available, or where a new site is necessary for the normal development of the business.
Under the terms of the act, a small business enterprise is that with an estimated annual gross revenue not exceeding $250,000. The maximum amount that can be borrowed at any time is $25,000 and loans are payable over a period of at most ten years. The maximum interest rate that can be charged on those loans is set by the regulations. It has been at 5J per cent since the beginning of this program.
The act became effective on January 19, 1961 for an initial period of about three years ending on December 31, 1964. It authorized the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to guarantee any bank against loss of an amount not exceeding 10 per cent of all the business improvement loans granted by the bank over the lending period. Provision was made for a total of $300 million for all loans that chartered banks could grant under the act during the lending period. The act was amended in 1963 so as to provide an additional three year lending period during which guaranteed loans could be made under the

DEBATES	February 16. 1967
same conditions as during the original lending period. The legislation now before the house will provide for another lending period which will extend from January 1, 1967 to January 31, 1969. During this further period, the same guarantee provisions will continue to apply just as during each of the two previous guarantee periods.
Due to the pressure of current business in the house, it was not possible to introduce the resolution preceding this bill before the middle of December 1966 and the schedule of legislation precluded discussion before the Christmas and New Year adjournment. In order to prevent stoppage of the operations being conducted under this legislation, the bill carries a clause making the application of this legislation retroactive to January 1, 1967. Meanwhile, the Minister of Finance has asked the chartered banks to continue lending under the act, pending the passage of the present bill and the minister has been assured by the banks that they would.
The other provisions of the bill concern the scope of lending operations under the Small Businesses Loans Act. They deal with points which may have contributed to the little use made of that act until now.
Every year from the implementation of the act until 1965, chartered banks have granted some 3,000 loans to small businesses, totalling $26 million. Although the final figures for 1966 are not yet available, it seems at first glance that loans in 1966 totalled $21 million. Therefore, during the six first years the act has been in operation an approximate total of $150 million has been granted in loans. Of course, it is not an unimportant amount and it has probably been quite beneficial to borrowers. But it might be possible that it is not a valid sign of the entire potential demand which could exist for such loans.
The rather moderate application of this act is mostly due to a few characteristics of its provisions and the purpose of this legislation is to amend those main features, in order to extend the application of the act to a greater number of small businesses.
A rather secondary factor, which explains the relatively limited use of this act, is the fact that the purposes for which loans could normally be granted included improvement or extension of premises. As I said earlier, the act admitted only the purchase or the building of replacement premises, when the premises used up to then were no longer available. Unusual situations arose from that. For example, the owner of a retail store
February 16, 1967	COMMONS
operating in rented space was not able, under the act, to finance the purchase of the building in which he had settled down, although he could, under the same act, finance the purchase of a building across the street if he was to evacuate the premises he was occupying. The new bill aims at extending the present grounds for loans, in order to allow the purchase and the construction of premises in every case and not only under the circumstances I just mentioned.
Another more significant factor is that the loans at present can only be granted to the small businesses engaged in manufacturing, wholesale, retail, and service. There are several other small businesses engaged in construction, transportation and communications that are not at present eligible for loans, under the act, but the nature of which would permit them to avail themselves of such loans, as well as the retailer or the small manufacturer. The bill provides eligibility to guaranted loans for the small business enterprises falling into these three classes.
A third factor is the present limitation on the size of the small business for eligibility. Such enterprise was defined as having an annual gross revenue not exceeding $250,000. Sometimes, particularly in the case of some retailers and wholesalers, this led to an arbitrary exclusion of businesses which, in other respects, could have qualified for loans under this act. The legislation before us changes the definition of the small business eligible in determining that its estimated annual gross revenue shall not exceed $500,000.

BasePK: 2471880

Speech:
Mr. Chairman, I realize the wish of the committee to complete this resolution stage this evening. However, I wanted on behalf of this group to express our approval of the resolution, and to do so in a brief space of time.
I am well aware that small businesses provide two things which are becoming increasingly rare-personal service and neighbourhood convenience, two important items in today's world. We approve of the broadening of this act so as to extend its usefulness, but I should like to say that unless this parliament and the government do a few other things at the same time we may find, as often happens when small businesses are developed, that we are laying the groundwork for a national chain of some kind or other to take over. Often small businesses are sold rather swiftly, not because they do not make enough money but because of the frustrations of their owners as a result of government intervention.
I recall very vividly sitting down with a group of small businessmen at one time and asking them what was their main problem in this regard. There was a short pause, and then came the answer "Well, the government". I can think of a couple of examples. One is the requirement of making quarterly payments of income tax. When a small businessman just starting up business is asked to make quarterly payments of tax prior to the end of the year, with refusal to pay or tardiness in payment involving him in the payment of interest on money which I do not see how he can owe the government anyway, this puts him to some hardship. Another problem has been mentioned over and over again in this house and is created by the Canada Pension Plan, overpayments to which being not returnable to small businessmen. This is the kind of thing we should take care of at the same time as we take this forward step in broadening the terms of the act.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

DEBATES	February 16, 1967
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Mr. Mcllraiih (for Mr. Sharp) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-270, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister, no matter how far down the line that authority may be delegated this morning. I should like to put the question in this way. In view of reports from Washington that the Central Intelligence Agency has been financing students or student groups on campuses both in the United States and in foreign countries, does the government have any knowledge that any of the more than 3,000 United States students attending Canadian universities are financed directly or indirectly by the Central Intelligence Agency?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Skeena asked whether I would be in a position to make a detailed announcement about the matter of safety at sea and manning scales of ships.
I can say to him that there was a meeting last week in Vancouver on these subjects, as he knows, and it was agreed at that meeting that all parties would deal with the towboat industry as soon as the laker project is completed. The laker project is proceeding; the draft in relation to lake vessels is well advanced and will be distributed to those concerned on both sides of the industry for comment. I expect that this will be done in the next few weeks.

BasePK: 2472008

Speech:
There is that provision, but postal employees may not be classified in that category though naturally we cannot assume that. There is some concern in this regard, and I would urge the bargaining agents who elect this course of action to use extreme caution because there is a feeling among the people of Canada about this right that is now being legally given to certain groups of public employees. I surmise that very few groups will elect this course, but just the same the legal right is to be given under the provisions of this bill.
Since remarks have been made about the other two bills, C-180 and C-182, I should like to express very serious reservations about the right of the public service commission to hear appeals. I am satisfied that the public service commission will deal with such appeals in a fair and equitable manner, but that is not the point. The principle that an appeal shall be made to the body which makes the decision in the first place is one which will create the feeling among people that they are not getting a fair deal. This involves the principle that it must not only be fair, it must appear to be fair. A great number of civil servants have expressed some reservation regarding the fact that any appeal from dismissal or demotion will have to be made to the body which made the first decision. I hope even at this late date the minister will consider a provision to set up some other tribunal to which such appeals can be made.
I do not wish to repeat some of the arguments presented to the committee, but civil servants generally are apprehensive about this bill because of the mix-up in reclassification and red circling. The majority of civil servants think of this bill in the same context as the bargaining bill.
Another part of the bill which disturbs me a little, and the minister should be aware that this may cause trouble, is that part relating to certification of bargaining units. It is true that the committee approved a very important amendment to the effect that the board will have the right to change
13172	COMMONS
Public Service Collective Bargaining the bargaining unit to the occupational group that is approved by the public service commission, but the effect of these artificially set up bargaining units will disrupt organizations that have performed a very useful service for many years. For example, the custom and excise officers' association has been actively serving its members for the last 30 years, and it is most unlikely that this association will be allowed to continue as the bargaining agent.
We will support this bill, Mr. Chairman. I hope that after a year or so of operation the minister will take another look at it. This is a new attempt to do by legislation that which has been done in Great Britain by use and custom. The minister should keep a close watch on its operation and consult frequently with representatives of the public service with a view to making changes as they become necessary to the efficient operation of this very complicated measure.

As I indicated when we were discussing a previous clause, I have reservations with respect to clause 6 which I wish now to express. This clause deals with Governor Generals' warrants. It repeals a former section and re-enacts it substituting the President of the Treasury Board for the Minister of Finance.
Now I was brought up in the old school which believed that Governor Generals' warrants were evil in themselves and basically inconsistent with responsible government. I therefore intend to oppose the re-enactment of this provision. In my opinion it is an affront to parliament and to responsible government for any prime minister to seek dissolution of parliament without having secured from parliament financial provision for at least the election period.
The persistent use of Governor Generals' warrants in the past few years is a denial of the basic function of the House of Commons. Four times in 25 years parliament has been totally by-passed and ignored and the national administration financed over long periods through this undemocratic technique. In 1940 Mr. Mackenzie King persuaded Lord Tweedsmuir, improperly, in my view, to dissolve parliament at a time when no provision had been made for the public service until a new parliament might meet. As a result, there had to be massive resort to Governor Generals' warrants.
This precedent was followed in 1958 when Mr. Massey granted the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert a dissolution without consideration of the financial provisions still to be made, and resort was had to Governor Generals' warrants not only for that fiscal year but for the ensuing year. From that date things have gone from bad to worse. When the former government was defeated in this house in February 1963, no effort was made, despite some urging by ministers, to come back to the house the following day and ask for financial provision to tide the administration over until the new parliament could meet. So essential Canadian needs were financed by that government, and by the government which was elected on April 8, 1963, through Governor Generals' warrants, and this was done for many months.
Then, deliberately, in September, 1965, the present Prime Minister induced General Vanier to grant a dissolution without the House of Commons having made any financial provision whatever for the election period.
Once again resort was had to Governor Generals' warrants for a period of several months. Four times for extended periods on each occasion this house has been by-passed and ignored and I think this intolerable denial of the basic authority of the House of Commons is something which should be stopped.
I believe this provision ought not to be re-enacted and that the correct procedure before the dissolution of parliament at any time is for the government to come to the House of Commons and secure supply for the period that is likely to elapse before the next parliament meets. Until this is done, parliament ought not to be dissolved. I believe, as I say, that a Governor Generals' warrant is evil per se and on that ground I intend to oppose the re-enactment of this clause.

Small Businesses Loans Act Amendment which will be coming before us, in the discussion of which in the finance committee I have been privileged to participate, indicate that the chartered banks of Canada have a particular role in our economy. On the other side of the coin I think that the banking institutions of this country have a responsibility to Canadians and that responsibility extends as well to small businessmen. Some of the speeches made at the resolution stage by the hon. member for Wellington-Huron (Mr. Howe) and other Conservative members, as well as by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) and other members of the New Democratic Party, indicate that they have the same idea as I do that the banks have a moral obligation to help the small businessman. I cannot understand those in this house who believe they are helping the small businessman by setting the interest rate as low as possible. If they would talk to these businessmen on the week ends they would find that the barrier these people face is not the interest rate but how they can get their hands on money from the chartered banks or other institutions of which they are a little suspicious, perhaps unjustly so.
While I endorse the amendments I believe they in no way shape or form overcome the weaknesses which existed in the act, one of which is indicated by the reluctance of the chartered banks to co-operate or to live up to their moral obligations so that the small businessman in each community has a chance to grow. I would have liked to see some provision in the act which would have permitted small businesses to obtain funds for mergers with other small businesses. Big businesses merge and unify. Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank hon. members who have contributed to this debate. My reply will be brief. A good deal has been said about the size of loans and whether it would not be wise in this act to increase the limit above $25,000, just as we have increased the eligibility of businesses by increasing the volume of business that makes them eligible from $250,000 to $500,000.
It will interest the house to know that in the last three years the average size of a loan under this act has been less than $10,000, though the upper limit was $25,000. It is even more interesting to note that the great bulk of loans has been in the range $5,000 to $15,000, which shows that the upper limit of the size of loans has not been a particularly limiting factor. Indeed the demand has been for much smaller loans.
Somebody asked whether the proposed amendments had been discussed with the retail merchants. I can answer in the affirmative. The Retail Merchants Association of Canada made representations to the government that the upper limit should be $50,000 rather than $25,000. The association on examination, however, was unable really to substantiate the need for the increase in the upper limit. Indeed they said that they would consider an increase of much smaller proportions to be quite adequate.
We did consider the possibility of raising the limit above $25,000, but in the light of the figures I have given to the house I think it will be understood that we do not consider that this was a major factor affecting the usefulness of this legislation.
Various members have spoken about the rate of interest. There has been general support for greater flexibility in the interest rate, that the banks might be encouraged to make loans to businesses under the guarantee provided by the act. Until the Bank Act provisions
February 24, 1967	COMMONS

May I suggest to the house three general considerations that I believe are highly relevant and that will to a large extent govern the regulations when they are ultimately promulgated. Second, the rate must be lower than the rate at which banks normally lend to businesses by a differential wide enough to preclude the banks putting all small business loans under the guarantee.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is a personal centennial project designed to provoke discussion in depth of the state of parliamentary and responsible government in 1967. To achieve its aim of restoring the independence of private members of parliament, the bill has four features. It would abolish the royal power of dissolution and substitute fixed dates of elections, subject to the right of the House of Commons itself and not the Prime Minister to determine a different and earlier date.
Second, defeat of a government proposal would lead to an election only if the house itself so determined by resolution.
A third and concomitant provision of the bill is that the House of Commons would have continuous legal existence, and in case of international or national crises parliament could be called into session even during an election campaign.
Finally, parliament would be required to make financial provision for the administration during an election period, and governor general's warrants would be abolished. The bill would apply to the twenty eighth and suDsequent parliaments.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

It establishes a profit sharing plan with a number of employees who are also shareholders and it pays certain sums into that plan. It has tame trustees. It then invests in the shares of a company, which in turn buys the bonds of the company that has established the profit sharing plan, and in the end the company that has established the profit sharing plan never pays the bonds. All that has happened is that the company has had the use of tax free funds without any benefit to anyone except the company itself and its shareholders, with a resulting loss to the treasury.
I do not see how such a situation can be dealt with unless there is a requirement that the company change its investments. This amendment provides that the Minister of National Revenue or an official or authorized person, as defined in section 133 of the act, may appeal an order or direction made by a court to require the minister or official to give evidence or produce information relating to information received under the Income Tax Act. But seriously, Mr. Chairman, the minister says this proposal is objective because it sort of automatically takes into consideration certain statistical factors which occur.
From that point of view it is objective, but a much more important basis for reallocation
March 10, 1967

of funds is the question of need in the provinces. I appreciate that that, of course, is reflected to some extent in the provincial tax structure, but not necessarily so. You may easily have a provincial regime that does not meet need and does not impose taxes which it ought to have imposed in order to meet certain social needs. The result is that it will keep its level of revenue low and get more out of this arrangement. Whether that is a good thing for Canada is a different story, but my major aim in speaking-and this is not in criticism of the minister-is to ask whether this was considered at all, or whether any studies are being initiated to deal with it.
The major problem I see in all these proposals is that municipal revenues and taxes are ignored. When you had a comparison at one time of only three sources of revenue and gave them the weight for equalization purposes, and later only two sources of revenue, you were of course in a sense being arbitrarily selective as to the basis of your comparison. But the moment you go to all the sources of revenue in a province and submit them to a national average, I respectfully suggest you are not dealing with the whole problem when you do not include in that consideration the needs of the municipalities and the revenues which they have to raise.
I repeat that if you take only a few sources of revenue you are making an arbitrary decision and the rest is not counted; but the moment you try to erect a structure on a basis which pretends to include, and is intended to include the total revenues of each of the provinces, geared to the total average of all the provinces for the purposes of equalization to bring everybody up to that average, then if you ignore the increased cost of welfare, education and all the other activities which the municipalities have to perform you are ignoring a very important part of the taxes raised in this country.
I am particularly concerned about that, as I am sure are all other members, because as the result of our constitutional arrangements and for other reasons the municipalities are limited almost entirely to perhaps the worst kind of tax, the tax on the home owner, which is unrelated to need, which is ungraduated, and which in most cases is a very great hardship on the lower income people.
I do not know if the minister and his advisers have considered whether it is possible to take municipal revenues into account and get the municipal picture as part of the total picture we are comparing. If they have not, I would like to ask whether some studies will
Equalization Payments to Provinces be made in that direction. I do not think I misunderstand the situation in Canada in this case, and I do think it is an important matter about which to be concerned.

How can you be satisfied with the amount of money in circulation when they do not have enough money to buy what they have worked for and they still have to borrow when they are producing?

March 13, 1967
Bank of Canada Act
In other words, I was asking the minister why it is that, with all kinds of goods already produced, the people should still have to borrow to purchase them?
This is the reply I received from the minister:
Mr. Chairman, the whole of our society is built on the foundation of credit. I am not at all happy that there is as much consumer credit in existence as there is, but every transaction in production nowadays involves some credit. Our system would not work very well if this were not so and I am, therefore, not concerned that there is a great volume of credit being used. This is, I think, normal. It is healthy and, indeed, unless there continues to be a rising volume of bank credit, then we would have good reason to be concerned about the future of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, this answer involves many things. The minister finds that healthy; he refers to the increase of the credit load of banks. He says it is logical that our society should be based on such a system, which he finds normal, and he wants this bank credit to continue to increase.

The process of credit creation is a familiar one.
You will note, Mr. Chairman, that in his first answer the Minister of Finance thought that this credit increase was normal and healthy.
In his reply to the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac, the minister explained how credit was created and he told us:
The process of credit creation is a familiar one. The banks make loans. The proceeds are left on deposit with the banks. They become part of the money supply. That is one way in which they are created. It is a familiar method.
The process of credit creation, I repeat it, because it is very important. It is the minister's answer as found on page 3012 of Minutes of Proceedings No. 43 and I repeat it:
The process of credit creation is a familiar one. The banks make loans.
The method used to create credit is simple: the banks make loans and when they do they create credit.
And I continue:
The proceeds are left on deposit with the banks. They become part of the money supply. That is one way in which they are created.

It is as clear as daylight, Mr. Chairman.

It appears that during the last 15 years a flexible reserve of between 8 and 12 per cent has been in existence in accordance with the Bank Act. The evidence before the committee showed that although during all those years there was the possibility of change, it was in fact unnecessary to do so. The other reserves were fixed on the basis of persuasion and varied from time to time in accordance with the wishes of the governor of the Bank of Canada. The banks themselves agreed to vary their secondary reserves.
One of the recommendations of the committee covers a multitude of sins in connection with the Bank Act. It is only fair to say there are a good many things we cannot anticipate because we do not know what the future will bring. With the idea, therefore, that experience will teach us along the way, the committee suggested in its report-I should like to read this recommendation in order to bring some substance to the position I take-that a different approach be made. It said:
Your committee recognizes the value of regular or decennial revisions of the Bank Act, the Bank of Canada Act, and the Quebec Savings Banks Act but believes that these should not prevent this committee carrying out special studies on subjects related to these Acts, and amendments being made to them from time to time if such become necessary in the interval.
We could dispute long and loud in this committee on many fine points with regard to which we have no experience which would enable us to form an opinion whether we were indeed taking the best possible course. The recommendations of the committee, if carried out, would meet this problem. As soon as it was found that something in the Bank Act needed revision the necessary adjustments could be made. It lays down the provisions under which banks may make loans to farmers. One of the difficulties which farmers face is that in many instances the manner in which their products are sold causes great concern and grave economic hardship. This is particularly true in regard to certain specialized crops such as fruits and vegetables and products of the dairy industry. These foods are financed and produced by the farmers and delivered to warehouses or storage facilities where they are subject to further processing before they are placed before the buying public.
In the case of dairy products, for example, milk is manufactured into cheese. When this takes place a long period of time often elapses between the time the primary producer delivers his goods and they pass out of his hands until the time he is paid for his product. Very often a tremendous risk is involved because of the perishable nature of the product and varying marketing conditions. There are instances where a farmer may deliver a product such as tomatoes and three or four months pass before he receives payment for his produce. I have used the example of milk products where there may be a lapse of 30 days or more before the farmer receives remuneration. In the case of tobacco and sugar beets, many months pass before the producer is paid for his product.

Second, there is grave concern that in many instances manufacturers may fall into economic chaos or bankruptcy before payment has been made. In extreme cases, the result has been that when

I meant to say comptroller general. Up to a point shortly before the 15th of July, I thought we were on the right road. I found that the tried and true channels of communication which had been the warp and woof of navy, army and air force procedures in chain of command for decades had largely been discarded. I found that officers working for me knew more, or said they knew more, or thought they knew more, about what was in the mind of the minister than I did. As hon. members will recall, the establishment of this Anglo-Canadian ministerial committee was agreed upon by the two

governments last year. While there are many occasions for British and Canadian ministers to meet, at Commonwealth gatherings at the United Nations and in a variety of other international bodies, it was felt that a joint ministerial committee could usefully supplement existing channels of communication and provide a most valuable means of consultation between the two governments. In this time of rapid change in Europe and the world at large it seemed to us that a committee of this kind with Britain, our second largest trading partner, would be especially useful and timely. As hon. members are aware, we have similar joint committees with the United States and with Japan.
Our experience has been that periodic ministerial meetings of this kind provide a unique opportunity for frank and intimate exchanges of views on a wide range of international and bilateral matters of common concern, and contribute to a better understanding of respective policies and problems.
I believe my colleagues on the delegation would agree that the new Anglo-Canadian ministerial committee got off to a good start, and that the very frank and cordial character of the discussion amply fulfilled our expectations. As indicated in the communique, British and Canadian ministers reviewed major current international issues including Viet Nam and the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons at the opening session at 10 Downing street under the chairmanship of Prime Minister Wilson. On that occasion there was also an exchange of views on the present situation with regard to Britain's possible approach to the European economic community and the important implications of this issue for Britain and Europe, for the world trading community as a whole and for trade between Canada and Britain. It was agreed that consultations on this subject would continue.
At its subsequent sessions in Marlborough House the committee discussed international and bilateral trade and economic matters including prospects for the economies of both countries; international liquidity; developments in the Kennedy round of trade and tariff negotiations including discussions of a multilateral cereals agreement; trade and aid for developing countries, including food aid, the prospects for a second United Nations conference on trade and development and development assistance in the Commonwealth, notably in the Caribbean area; and a variety of bilateral trade matters.
It was agreed that the committee would hold its second meeting in Canada at a date to be determined later.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution of congratulations which you have just read and which, as you have said, was moved in the British House of

Commons by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, was passed unanimously by that ancient and illustrious body which two years ago celebrated its seven hundredth anniversary in the same hall at Westminster where it first met.
Very generous remarks were made when this resolution was being considered at Westminster by the Prime Minister, Right Hon. Harold Wilson, by the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Heath, and by the leader of the Liberal party, Mr. Thorpe. I am sure all members of this house share my appreciation of this generous and friendly gesture, and I am sure that all members would wish this appreciation to be suitably expressed and recorded, for transmission to Westminster.
As has been the case with many countries, we inherited our own parliamentary institutions from Britain, the home of the mother of parliaments. Indeed, one of the bonds holding together that unique organization, the Commonwealth of Nations, is this shared parliamentary heritage.
In Canada, parliamentary institutions have played a vital part in the development of our Confederation. They have served us faithfully and well in war and peace, in bad times and in good. They have enabled our country to grow with a maximum degree of freedom for our people, and with a maximum of consideration for discussion and dissent in the solution of our problems. It is difficult to imagine a more stable or suitable governmental foundation for future progress as we contemplate our second century of confederation. The capacity of our parliamentary system to adjust itself in response to the requirements of the moment, without sacrificing its basic characteristics, has been demonstrated in the past. We must hope that the subtle, durable mechanism, of which this house forms such an important part, will successfully meet the even more difficult and important challenges of the present by adapting itself to the new conditions we face.
We often forget that it was the combined genius of Anglo-Saxon and Norman French that brought about the birth and development of the parliamentary system in Britain. In Canada there has been a similarly enriching association of these two races in our parliamentary evolution. In working out our federal system of government, parliamentary institutions have enabled English speaking and French speaking Canadians to settle their problems and find acceptable accommodations for their difficulties in a framework
May 8, 1967	COMMONS
of rational discussion and intelligent cooperation.
I feel confident that we can look forward to continued steady parliamentary progress, and that we shall not betray the great achievements of the last hundred years or prove unworthy of the generous sentiments that the resolution of the British House of Commons so graciously emphasizes.
In introducing this resolution into the House of Commons at Westminster, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom quoted the words of Lord Carnarvon, the Colonial Secretary of the day, when he moved second reading of the British North America Act in 1867. He said then:
We are laying the foundation of a great state

perhaps one which, at a future day, may even overshadow this country. But, come what may, we shall rejoice that we have shown neither indifference to their wishes nor jealousy of their aspirations, but that we honestly and sincerely, to the utmost of our power and energy, fostered their growth, recognizing in it the conditions of our own greatness.
It is good to know that the British House of Commons, 100 years later, continues to have these same generous and warm feelings about our country.
It is my pleasure and my honour to move, seconded by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, the following resolution:
That this house, acknowledging the Resolution of the British House of Commons, conveying most friendly greetings and warm congratulations on the centenary of the establishment of the Canadian House of Commons, and all good wishes for the second century of its existence;
Recalling the unfailing good will extended to it by the British House of Commons at the time of confederation, and throughout the century that has followed;
Mindful that parliamentary institutions, our heritage from the mother of parliaments, have served Canada well during the past hundred years;
Requests Mr. Speaker to express to the British House of Commons sincere and grateful appreciation for its kind greetings and congratulations.

I am privileged to participate in this debate after the very thoughtful contribution which has just been made by the hon. gentleman who preceded me. The hon. member for York South must have exactly the same sense of humour, because the subamendment he introduced is of precisely the same character. It represents a vote of non-confidence in the policy of the government on a matter of very great importance indeed. We do not propose at this time to accept this subamendment because it represents, as the hon. gentleman who has just preceded me pointed out, a onesided approach to this problem. It deals with one aspect alone of that problem, though I agree it is an important one.
The view behind the subamendment is that we are not dealing with a case of aggression from the north, that in Viet Nam, as the hon. member put it yesterday, there is merely a civil war and that the United States had no right to be there from the beginning. In the hon. member's words-I took them from Hansard because I did not have the pleasure of hearing the whole of his interesting speech- "the world's mightiest power has intervened in a local situation". He went on to point out that Hanoi, on the other hand, had limited its activities in Viet Nam and had bombed nobody. On the basis of this statement and others he made he adjures us as follows: "Let us recognize these facts. What right has the United States to be there in that situation?" This, I believe, is the basis of his approach, and the approach of those who feel as he does.
I believe that the purposes and objectives of United States policy in Viet Nam were not aggression. I believe that the United States moved into Viet Nam in the first place to help South Viet Nam, at the invitation of the government of that country, to defend itself against military action and subversive terrorism aimed at preventing the people of that part of Viet Nam making their own decision
Foreign Policy
as to their future development and political institutions rather than having one particular solution forced upon them under the guise of a liberation struggle conducted in the interests of a totalitarian communist regime in North Viet Nam which has not allowed and does not intend to allow its own people any choice as to their social, economic or political system.
Mr. Bundy, who played an important part in these matters in earlier days as adviser on foreign affairs to the president, has written these words:
United States policy remains based on the continuing conviction that we should be ready to do our full share to help prevent the communists from taking south Viet Nam by force and terror.
We may not agree with this policy, but I think those words are a rational explanation of the policy followed by men in the United States who are men of good will and as peace loving as we are. I can understand their position in this regard. That does not mean a government in Canada has to support or approve all the measures taken or all the measures adopted by the United States forces in Viet Nam, let alone by the governments in Saigon-and remember there have been more governments than one-in achieving their purposes. And on occasions when I have felt it necessary to speak publicly and not confine myself to diplomacy-I do not care very much for the phrase "quiet diplomacy"; if diplomacy is to be any good it is bound to be quiet-I have made this clear.

I still regret it. I think it was a great mistake on the part of the United States administration at that time to resume the bombing in the circumstances in which it was resumed. izing exports of military equipment to countries in that area. Some exports of parts for non-combat piston aircraft and non-combat vehicles received authorization after careful consideration.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-105 replaces Bill S-52 introduced in the other place. That bill subsequently received second reading in this house on April 25 of this year. It was referred to the standing committee on transport and communications where it remained to the end of last session.
When Bill S-52 was introduced in the other place the sponsor had this to say:
... the sponsors desire that it be made clear that this proposed federal pipe line, as is the case with the existing Alberta pipe line, will serve all producers in the area without discrimination. These lines will not be limited to the carriage of oil belonging to the four companies which are sponsoring this application.
It should be pointed out that the sponsors of this company, Mobil Oil Canada Limited, Imperial Oil Limited, Aquitaine Company of Canada and Banff Oil Limited, are desirous of being in a position to offer facilities for the transportation of oil to areas in the Northwest Territories north of the Alberta boundary as soon as sufficient production develops. As the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange) has already indicated, it is suspected that the oil bearing formation apparent in Alberta follows a line straight through the Northwest Territories to the Arctic circle.
The bill now under consideration would provide for an extension into the Northwest Territories to serve anticipated production in that region. As pointed out by the hon. member, there is a pipe line which extends almost to the boundary of the Northwest Territories, owned, controlled and operated by a company with a similar name, although it is an Alberta incorporated company.
The company we are now considering would be ready to provide facilities if as and when the level of production warranted the extension of the pipe line now constructed in the Rainbow lake area of northern Alberta. This company would operate under the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board in the
Private Bills
same way as other oil and gas pipe line operators. A new feature has been added. This company requests the power and authority to do all the things that an oil exploration and development company would be expected to do, namely, to acquire and hold leases, prospect for oil and gas, drill for and produce oil, gas and related substances.
There are several aspects of this undertaking, including the one I just mentioned, which should be given careful consideration by this house. This would require too much time at this stage of the bill and I believe it can be given the thorough examination it deserves only in committee. We hope the committee on transport and communications will have the opportunity to examine this bill and, if it is thought necessary, to call and hear witnesses. We do not want to block this legislation because we realize that pipe lines are the life lines of the oil industry. However, the present bill not having been examined by the committee yet, we can only accept second reading at this time on division.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to reform and improve the bail system of Canada. As is set forth in the explanatory notes of the bill, the measure aims-
-to asure that all persons, regardless of their financial status, shall not needlessly be detained pending their appearance to answer charges under acts of the Parliament of Canada, when detention serves neither the ends of justice nor the public interest.
This measure will permit poor people awaiting trial to be released without bond and will thus eliminate the arbitrary cruelty in the present bail system.
The no-bail release system established by this bill is limited to instances where the offence is not punishable by death or life imprisonment and in which the judge deems the defendant trustworthy.
The bill will also assure that persons convicted of crimes and infractions will receive credit for time spent in custody prior to trial against service of any sentence imposed by the court.
I intend to outline very briefly the detailed amendments proposed to the Criminal Code in line with the aim of this bill and also in line with the safeguarding of the powers of the court to compel the appearance of an accused. First however I would like to remind hon. members that the bill follows almost precisely the trail blazed last year in the United States when the President signed similar legislation into effect with these words:
It is a move to ensure that defendants are considered as individuals and not as dollar signs.
That our Canadian scales of justice are sometimes weighted not with mercy but with money has been apparent in the matter of before trial detention. A very detailed study of the situation was made in 1965 by M. L. Friedland of the faculty of law of the University of Toronto. I should like to quote briefly from the writings of Mr. Friedland. This is what he wrote:
In the setting of bail there is an undue preoccupation with its monetary aspects. The tragedy is that a large percentage of persons are unable to raise the bail that is set (two-thirds according to the Toronto study). The ability of the accused to marshal funds or property in advance determines whether he will be released and may have an effect on the outcome of his case.
The professional bondsmen and moneylenders operate more or less openly, and in my
Bail Reform
opinion their operations are open to criticism. Actually, the system does not do too much to ensure the appearance of the accused in court, and the people who lend the money reap substantial profits. Some accused, in order to raise the money, commit further offences while awaiting trial. The system tends to favour the professional criminal, who is more likely to know and be trusted by the professional bondsmen.
It seems to me that here is a field which requires reform. I would say that if money rather than character is not to determine justice, the accused should be released, if he is to be released at all, on his own recognizance, or, in appropriate cases, with recognizances by sureties in reasonable amounts recoverable if the accused fails to appear.
The bill which I am proposing as a means to meet and reform the existing bail system would make these specific changes in the Criminal Code, and I quote from the text of the bill:
...any person charged with an offence under an Act of the Parliament of Canada, other than an offence punishable by death or imprisonment for life, shall at his appearance in court, be ordered released pending trial on his personal recognizance or upon the execution of an unsecured appearance bond in an amount specified by the court, unless the judge determines, in the exercise of his discretion, that such a release will not reasonably assure the appearance of the person as required.
3. (1) When a judge makes such a determination, he shall, either in lieu of or in addition to the methods of release referred to in section 2, impose the first of the following conditions of release which will reasonably assure the appearance of the person for trial or, if no single condition gives that assurance, any of the combination of the following conditions:
(a)	place the person in the custody of a designated person or organization agreeing to supervise him;
(b)	place restrictions on the travel, association, or place of abode of the person during the period of release;
(c)	require the execution of an appearance bond in a specified amount and the deposit in the registry of the court, in cash or other security as directed, of a sum not to exceed 10 per centum of the amount of the bond, such deposit to be returned upon the performance of the conditions of release;
(d)	require the execution of a bail bond with sufficient solvent sureties, or the deposit of cash in lieu thereof; or
(e)	impose any other condition deemed reasonably necessary to assure appearance as required, including a condition requiring that the person return to custody after specified hours.
Clause 4 of the bill reads:

The most impressive and significant aspect of this meeting was without

doubt the forward looking nature of the discussions and the spirit of cordiality and of genuine good will which prevailed. These discussions have proven fruitful and will be of benefit in our day-to-day continuing contacts with the United States government over the weeks and months ahead. This I personally believe is their great merit.
As will be apparent from the communique, the committee considered a wide range of important topics of interest to Canada and the United States in the trade, economic and financial fields. These included broad policy issues of a multilateral character in which both our countries have a vital stake and important responsibilities. In addition, a major portion of our discussions was concerned with subjects of special interest in our bilateral relations.
In the forward looking context of the meeting, emphasis was placed on the opportunities for trade which will be presented by the results of the Kennedy round and we agreed to work closely together in studying further trade liberalization opportunities.
In a number of important areas, including co-operation in wheat marketing policies and food aid, the committee decided to strengthen the consultative arrangements between the two countries. On other issues where there are outstanding problems between Canada and the United States, each side had an opportunity to explain its case fully and frankly and to explore the possibilities of early accommodation.
I need not review at this time the many issues that were jointly examined, and which are outlined in the communique. I would, however, refer to one or two particular topics.
As will be seen from the communique, a very close identity of interest was recorded in the matter of the approach of the two countries to the problem of international liquidity and the need for general agreement on a contingency plan for reserve expansion.
We had a most useful exchange of views on the important question of foreign investment in Canada. This meeting provided a further opportunity for Canadian ministers to reemphasize the government's intention to maintain a favourable climate for foreign investment in Canada, while encouraging increased Canadian participation in the control and ownership of our economy.
Special attention was also devoted to the important question of energy resources between the two countries. The United States
June 23. 1967

cabinet members gave us a welcome re-affirmation of United States recognition of the important role of oil in our over-all trade and economic relationship, and of their continued interest in enabling Canada to share in the growth of the United States market.
Canadian ministers again took the opportunity to mention the concern felt in Canada about the extra-territorial application of the laws of other countries. At the same time we noted the readiness of United States secretaries to use their best endeavours to resolve particular problems in this area if and when they arise.
This meeting of the ministerial committee will, I am sure, contribute significantly to the atmosphere of co-operation and mutual understanding within which we can best hope to resolve the complex and difficult problems which from time to time arise between the world's two largest trading partners.
May I say that it was a particular pleasure to welcome United States cabinet members and their wives to the great city of Montreal and to have them visit Expo '67 in this centennial year. I wish in conclusion to thank my colleagues and the large number of Canadian officials who participated both in the preparatory work and in the meeting itself for their splendid co-operation.

She has said that these are the only grounds which she will consider for rejection. It would appear that the problem in Sydney arises from a number of factors, including some softening in the market not only in Canada but in most countries for some of the kinds of steel which Dosco Steel Limited produces. Because the Sydney plant is at a considerable distance from the main Canadian markets for steel, the company faces keen competition from most other domestic producers who are closer to these markets. The company reports that it has been rationalizing its operations in order to improve its ability to meet increased competition from Canadian
June 27, 1967	COMMONS
and other producers, and this also has affected the situation.
Furthermore, faced with increasing competition and declining prices in its main marketing areas the company says it has taken steps to improve the productivity of its operations at Sydney which have resulted in some curtailment of the numbers employed.
In addition, there is a world-wide overcapacity of steelmaking facilities, and imports of certain steel products into the areas of Canada which are readily accessible by sea have been increasing. These areas are also the main markets in which products made from Sydney steel are sold. It has been said by Dosco that some of the imports may involve dumping and the Department of National Revenue has been asked to undertake an appropriate investigation as quickly as possible.
It is evident from these facts that the problem in Sydney relates not only to general market factors, but equally it relates to special problems for this company. In these circumstances, the government has come to the view that stockpiling of Sydney steel does not provide a solution to either of these problems. Moreover it would not be an appropriate measure for the federal government to initiate in these circumstances.
We do not believe, however, that there is a long term general problem in Canada affecting the steel industry as a whole. Rather, the problems affecting the steel operations in Sydney, although aggravated by the current market situation, appear to be of a special nature.
Because of the complexity of the problem it would seem to me that if a thorough study of the steel industry in Cape Breton were available, this would make it easier for the responsible authorities to examine the problem in a more informed way.

made in such a way as to gain the maximum political advantage, and this was done carefully and deliberately. This has caused a greater spiralling of construction costs, including the construction of hospitals, than anything else.
An examination of these grants should have been made long ago. With the implementation of full medicare and the resulting demands that will be made on the hospitals of this country, it is scandalous that no changes have been made in the schedule of these grants. When the people read the statements of the minister regarding his promises for medicare they will be lulled into the false assurance that their medical needs will be taken care of after 1968. However, when they go or attempt to be admitted to hospital after 1968 they will learn that space is simply not available. Whether or not doctors will be available is doubtful, but the space will not be available and medicare will be meaningless for them because the groundwork has not been laid. They will be victims of the same illusion that some of the old age security pensioners laboured under when they accepted the promises that some of their problems would be alleviated by this government but later learned to their sorrow that promises and the implementation of them are not always the same.
Finally I should like to refer to what is perhaps a minor part of the spending of the department, that on grants for fitness and amateur sport. We in this country are proud of our contribution to amateur sport and our efforts in a great many fields, some of which we consider particularly Canadian. We have been particularly proud of our efforts in the field of hockey and extremely proud of our recent ski teams. However, compared to what happens in many nations of the world, our approach to these things on the governmental level cannot even be considered amateurish, but only rather infantile.
In this respect, although we had a sharp increase from 1964 to 1967 in the estimates

We know there are any number of governments in the world which set out deliberately as national policy to have the finest teams of athletes to take part in various competitions in the world that they can possibly send. We send our teams and, with rare exception, we are disappointed with the results. The savings associated with the cost of constructing two ships in each of two yards as opposed to the cost of constructing one ship in each of four yards is appreciable. What the difference actually is is difficult to determine because it would be necessary to call tenders side by side in the two different manners in order to know precisely what it is. We are still in the process of negotiating a settlement in a number of areas. Until the negotiations are complete we will not be able to give precise figures. The members of this party are extremely disturbed that the house should propose to adjourn for a summer recess without dealing with the matter which has been raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). have been months of delay. We have been told that the matter was under active, serious and urgent consideration. Consideration has been given to it every time but no action is ever taken.

Speech:
In 1931 the name Harrington lake was approved by the Geographic Board of Canada when the names for a map of the area were being considered. There was no controversy at that time as the name Harrington was found to be firmly established on all maps examined.
In 1951 an article in the Ottawa Journal suggesting that a more historically appropriate name would be Lac Mousseau prompted an inquiry by the Canadian board on geographical names, the predecessor of the present Canadian permanent committee on geographical names. The matter was investigated much more thoroughly than in 1931. It was ascertained that the name Harrington appeared on many maps and plans dating back to 1850 on a surveyor's plan of the area. The name Harrington appears to have been applied by this surveyor and may have resulted from the land grant in 1827 to a Joseph Harrington of lot 19 in the 6th range of Hull, some six miles south of the lake, according to evidence furnished by the Public Archives of Canada. Additional evidence served to confirm that the Harrington family occupied land near the lake until after the middle of the century. Letters were received from local
Questions
residents, mainly cottagers, supporting the name Harrington.
The name Lac Mousseau was promoted by others just as strongly stating that Louis Mousseau settled on the shore of the lake in 1867, his descendants retained title until at least 1905, and that most people have known the lake by this name for the past 50 to 60 years.
After a full review of the evidence and representations, the board decided in 1951 to retain the name Harrington. The decision was based mainly on the long establishment of the name on maps and plans as well as on demonstrated local usage. The board recognized that the name Lac Mousseau was also used, but they did not see fit to adopt the double name.
In Bill C-64, 1959, amending the Prime Minister's Residence Act, the lake is designated as Harrington lake (Lac Mousseau) in the English text and Lac Mousseau (Harrington lake) in the French text.
On September 5, 1962 a draft copy of topographic map 31 G/12d published by this department was forwarded to Quebec for a names check. On December 18, 1962, a letter was received from the secretary of the Quebec geographical board stating that the Quebec minister of lands and forests had approved the name Lac Mousseau (Lac Harrington). This name was ratified by the Canadian permanent committee on geographical names and is the official name of the lake.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution could be mere windowdressing, a hollow faqade, or it could represent a move toward a constructive and intelligent community involvement in the significant work of the Department of Manpower and Immigration at the national, regional and local levels. The minister's brief and relatively uninformative statement this afternoon certainly gave us no indication which of these alternatives is likely to result from the resolution before us. Consequently it seems to me we must defer judgment and await the bill itself for a more elaborate explanation of its purpose before reaching a final conclusion.
I wish to make only two comments at this stage. The first is that the more community involvement there can be in government procedures at this level, the better it will be for government and the better it will be for manpower policy generally. We are in the days of big government-I fear this is inevitable-and it is more than ever important to get at local and regional levels a genuine committee involvement of dedicated persons who are prepared to give their time and energy in helping to formulate policy. This is important even at the staffing level.
One of the results of the creation of the new Canada manpower centres has been grave dissatisfaction on the part of the staff in some of these offices. I hope the minister will do something soon to remove the discrimination which exists as a result of the policies of his department and the policies of the Public Service Commission. I say to him this afternoon as we resume this session of parliament that unless decisive action is taken to remove discrimination against public servants in various offices of the manpower centres across the country he will have a tough time before the session ends.
With respect to the minister's observations about the local committees being involved in
DEBATES	2441
Manpower and Immigration Council the adjustment of immigrants to Canada, I think the minister would agree with me that we have not done as much as we ought to have done in this connection nor has there been sufficient co-ordination at the provincial and municipal levels. I hope that settlement policies will in future be co-ordinated more closely than has been the case at any time in the past. I, for one, will be looking forward to what I hope will be constructive results from these local committees which are to deal, in the words the minister used, with the adjustment of immigrants to Canada.
The second point I should like to make is that I am concerned lest under this proposal for a Canada manpower and immigration council, immigration policy may become subordinate or subservient to manpower policy. This, the minister may remember, is precisely the fear I expressed at the time the reorganization bill was under discussion in the house when the Department of Manpower and Immigration was created-a fear lest immigration policy might become at all times conditioned exclusively to what might be the economic circumstances or the economic whims within this country during a particular period.
This committee and the house have listened frequently to my contention that immigration is a stimulus to the economy, that it is a genuine stimulus in a period of economic recession just as it is in a period of economic growth. I reject completely any tap on, tap off policy or any attempt to relate long-range immigration objectives to immediate changes in our economic climate. So the warning I give this afternoon as the minister introduces his resolution is clear and definitive. I hope he will give us his assurance, and I hope the council will remember, that it is not the intention of this house that immigration policy shall be merely subservient to manpower policy and that we should only bring in immigrants when there are precise places available for their employment.
I disagree with the view expressed a short time ago by the hon. member for Chapleau. I believe it is a shortsighted view, one which will not permit this country to grow as rapidly as it ought. We need to set targets and objectives for immigration and go forward to meet those goals in the belief that the very bringing in of immigrants in maximum numbers will provide employment for more people in this country by providing an important stimulus.

A means can and must be found to cut through the red tape and to put an end to the buck-passing among the three levels of government which has limited action up to the present time. I suggest to the members of this house that the most fundamental reason why federal public housing funds have not been fully used up to the present time is that additional public housing in the large urban municipalities such as Toronto, which need public housing most, will under existing conditions impose an additional, unwarranted and indeed unbearable burden on the home owner. Independent studies make it entirely clear the urban home owner at the present time is bearing an unfair and regressive tax burden. If Toronto or any other urban municipality wishes to use federal public housing funds, it must be prepared to put up a small percentage of the capital cost itself. It is a small percentage but it does involve some additional burden.
Much more important, however, are the hidden charges upon the municipality resulting from public housing. These include the cost of providing water mains, sewage systems and municipal services of all kinds, and particularly schools for the large numbers of children in the public housing projects. Again federal legislation makes federal money available for certain services such as sewage systems. Nevertheless, public housing does impose an additional and unfair burden upon the municipal taxpayer. Moreover, municipal

September 28. 1967
Supply-Labour
resources are limited, and in these circumstances it is only natural and human that municipal officials will encourage the construction of revenue-producing office buildings and industrial plants rather than public housing projects. Surely it is entirely clear that if the municipalities are to welcome public housing projects these projects must be made financially attractive to the municipalities. This is a financial, not a constitutional, problem and it can be solved.
Out of date municipal building restrictions and expropriation laws also impede public housing. Finally, the additional time and expense involved in dealing with a multitude of authorities at three different governmental levels impose a heavy and often impossible burden of expense, delay and frustration upon all those concerned with public housing.
No doubt these problems can be resolved in a number of ways. However, any solution does involve more direct federal participation in public housing and therefore a new federal initiative in this field. For example, in each large urban municipality where a serious public housing problem exists there could be formed under provincial charter a public housing corporation governed by a small and competent board of directors consisting of persons nominated by the municipality and the provincial and federal governments. I hope these persons would not be civil servants. Our civil service bureaucracy is already too large.
The necessary money would be provided by the federal and provincial governments in the agreed ratios. The corporation would have the power to expropriate on fair terms, power to cut through unreasonable municipal building restrictions, to acquire and service raw land and to buy or build public housing.
Admittedly there is need now for economy in government, but this plan would not involve expenditures above those now contemplated. Some of the money previously used to finance expensive single family homes would be diverted to meet the needs of those people whose needs are greatest and most urgent. not the best ultimate solution. October 5, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Davis process we will improve our productivity. The Economic Council of Canada has been harping on the question of productivity, and well it might. We need to improve our output per man-hour. We can do this if people move to areas of greater opportunity, to growth areas with new industries. In these areas the latent abilities of people could really be put to work.
There are many initiatives which I should like to see the federal government take in the months and years ahead. I should like to see us not only set up a department of urban affairs or a department of housing and urban affairs, or whatever the title may be, but one which would deal with more than just being the banker for people who need housing. I should like to see the federal government enter even more into the planning process with the municipalities.
I should like to see such a department help to solve not just the housing problems of people but their transportation problems, their sewage disposal problems, and so on. I should like to see the department deal with the provision of services primarily through its banking function. In effect, the money would be lent and it would be paid back by the users. It would be directly related to the value received. I think this is the businesslike way of doing things and I should like to see the federal government act more in this way.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the National Housing Act of this country have been great successes. These were federal initiatives in an area which the constitutional lawyer has always said was reserved to the provinces. Ottawa took the lead in the early 1940's. It established a building code. Many progressive municipalities adopted the code. Progressive municipalities, provincial governments and private organizations have joined in creating facilities which would not otherwise have existed. Shelter has been provided for people of different incomes and in all parts of the country. This has been all to the good.
In respect of transportation I should like to see the federal government do what has been done by the federal government of the United States. That government has built great highways, throughways, connecting streets and so on through a special fund. This fund has been developed by imposing a tax of roughly one cent per gallon on gasoline and diesel oil. The tax money accumulating in the fund is paid out to municipalities in order that they may build highways, throughways, connecting streets, etc. The federal authorities in the

United States make sure that there is adequate planning and they often help the municipalities to plan. Once the plans are agreed upon the federal government of the United States, through this fund, puts up as much as 90 per cent of the capital cost of all the new facilities they need.
We could at least go 50-50 with the municipalities, or the municipalities and/or the provincial governments. The user of these facilities the man paying the one cent a gallon tax, would be seeing the results of the tax turning up in terms of more efficient streets, better highways and less time lost in transit. I am sure he would get value for the money paid in the form of this tax. He would get value in the form of a lessening of the time taken to travel, reduction of the wear on tires, brake shoes, and so on. I am sure he would see a reasonable relationship between this tax and the facilities progressively made available to him. He would also see an account that would be in balance.
In putting such a program into effect we would be relating benefits much more directly to costs. This is the type of program that we need. We need it, by all means, with the help and blessing of the provinces, but I for one would not drag my feet and wait indefinitely for all the provinces to get on this bandwagon because, as the Economic Council of Canada has so clearly pointed out, the urban problem, the great movement of Canadians from outlying areas into our big cities, is going to be with us a long time.
We are reaching the point where 80 per cent of our people will be living in the great metropolitan areas. The figure will perhaps be 85 per cent by the turn of the century. So let us have a department that looks ahead in trying to solve the biggest single problem that we face. Let us have not just departments dealing with rural affairs and matters like ARDA and so on, praiseworthy as they may be, but a department that deals more with the really big problems of the future, problems that will involve many more people who will have even greater difficulties adjusting themselves to the circumstances in which they find themselves.

We are at war, and you should real se that fact. We have a war that must be fought against poverty. Many people need houses. Many young couples are being thrown out of apartment buildings because they have two or more children and landlords do not like to have children around. This may not appear to be a war to the minister, but it certainly is a war so far as those people who are struggling to maintain some sort of decent standard of living are concerned. I suggest that the minister take a very serious look at their plight instead of just saying that this is not a time of war. If we can muster our intelligence, resources and courage in order to devastate things, surely we can find some ingenuity to fight these problems of poverty.
The minister has said that solutions to our problems would not be easy to find. We must move away from reliance on past economic policies. We cannot continue to believe that if we wait things will adjust themselves. We have passed that point. Once we have committed ourselves to a full employment policy-and I do not see how any government could fail to follow such a policy-we must then go on further. We cannot turn the clock back to times of unemployment. We must talk about how to maintain prosperity and how to prevent inflation with full employment. In order to do this the government must bring in some measure of control over the economy.
There is no invisible hand to guide the destiny of the people. There are hands but they are not invisible-they are the hands of everyone looking toward his own interests. This may not be in the best interests of the people of this country, but it is the situation. There is no longer a question as to whether we are going to plan or not plan. The question now is, who is going to do the planning for us, the large corporations or the government. Are these large corporations to determine our economic future? I do not ask that question with any malevolence, but I feel that our economic future should be determined by the sovereign government elected by the people of this country. Does this government intend to sit here and suggest that it cannot interfere in these delicate matters, and
