I suggest that we will need a prices review board, selected price controls, restructuring of our industry and a changing emphasis from primary to secondary manufacturing. The government must maintain more control on our economy and import replacement. There must be a lessening of our dependence on United States markets in order that we may determine our own values with less inhibition. It is this government, or any other government that wishes to accept responsibility, which must determine the social priorities and investment priorities of this nation. The economy of the United States is still on the upswing and the editor of a leading market journal stated the other day that food prices in that country were about to increase once more. The independent grocer, the fellow in the comer store, has been eliminated. He does not count in this network of corporations controlled by giants. His interests and hands are tied. A few major chains are now in a position to exercise monopoly control in the hunt for profits. The hunt for profits is always a legitimate exercise of corporate enterprise, but a hunt for exorbitant and inordinately high profits is not. I am sure the minister is aware of this and I expect that the government wishes to come to grips with this problem.
This bill will not do that. This government,

Already inflation and unemployment have restricted the ability of private citizens to meet the commitments they have entered into and the government should be careful indeed about generating more restrictions of that kind.

DEBATES	November 20, 1967
In framing policies to deal with all these problems, in stating economic and social goals and in deciding how we are to try to achieve them, it is essential for the government to have the understanding, co-operation and support of the people generally. It is essential for it to have the co-operation, understanding and support of the organizations and mechanisms through which groups of people protect their own interests, attempt to influence the economy and obtain their own fair share, as they see it, from its progress.
I am not suggesting for a moment that the government must always have a consensus on details or even on major parts of some of the policies which it believes to be required by the economy. Certainly, sometimes governments must do unpalatable and unpopular things, unpalatable and unpopular in the short rim at least, so that the long term welfare of our people may be advanced and assured. I do not suggest that we must always have a consensus before the government is entitled to act. But as to the general objectives of government policy and as to the general objectives of social policy there must be co-operation and support and, most of all, these objectives and the means of obtaining them must be understood clearly and fully throughout the country by other governments, by labour and industry and by investors and consumers.
It is obvious that in a democracy this support and co-operation may be attained not by coercion but only by persuasion and by the persuasive force of example, leadership and consultation by the government of Canada.

This is inflation of the worst kind. This can affect the whole building industry. The economy cannot afford it.

It would be too lengthy a process to establish one to deal with this sort of situation. I believe it is time the minister considered something more effective than merely warning or pleading with these rapacious corporations to avoid adding to our economic difficulties; he should be consulting the provinces in which these companies are located and urging them to use their constitutional powers to establish price controls over these basic industries. Otherwise they will get completely out of hand.

The purpose of a royal commission is to get a number of different views. By appointing three, five or seven persons to a royal commission you would get these different views and then, by a process of distillation of opinion, the royal commissioners reach a consensus on some important social or economic problem which they have been asked to examine.
We must ask ourselves, who would replace the judges? The first group of people that come to mind would be the economists. It is said of economists that if you put three in a
November 24, 1967

room you get four opinions. If we made up a royal commission of economists, the taxpayers would get one opinion for nothing, so I think that would be a desirable saving to the taxpayers.
After giving the matter more thought, it seemed to me that if we were not going to allow judges to sit on royal commissions we should perhaps have royal commissions made up of newspaper publishers and editors. It seems to me there are a number of important benefits from this proposal. Of course if a royal commission were made up of newspaper publishers, we would be assured from the beginning that the royal commission would have the benefit of a wide range of views on any given subject into which the commission inquired. If one picks ten editorials on any given subject, he usually finds there are three editors in favour, three opposed, two editors usually have not decided on their position, and by the end of the editorial two more have managed not to declare themselves either for or against. Therefore, we have the advantage of being automatically guaranteed a wide range of opinion.
It seems to me therefore it would be very good for newspaper publishers and editors to be appointed royal commissioners. They would have to grapple with the problems of the nation, rather than sit in their offices and write editorials. This would be a good training for them. A more important benefit is that we would be automatically guaranteed editorial support for whatever recommendations the royal commission might make. As it is now, we have recommendations coming from royal commissions which cost us a great deal of money, and then the newspaper publishers across the country set about shooting down those recommendations in flames. If the recommendations were made by the publishers, then automatically when the royal commission report was made public it would receive the overwhelming support of the Canadian editorial writers. The recommendations would then be easily implemented by the government. I think we could solve the major issues of the nation in this way.

Inquiries Act Amendment which I am sure would solve the problem once and for all. From that point of view, among several others, of course.
That area over which I had the pleasure of flying last summer has been developed over quite a number of years. It will be recalled that in 1898, it was the scene of the Gold Rush; it will also be remembered that in 1943, the Alaska highway was built through it. But it is mostly since 1947, due to exploration work for gas and oil in the territories to the south and to the gradual extension of that exploration and development to the north, that this area has become important and will become even more so in the future.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of defining the land boundary rather than changing it.
As early as 1898, the federal Department of the Interior had started the work, which lasted from 1899 to 1908, but most of the surveying has been done since 1943. In that year, the Privy Council, with the agreement of British Columbia, instituted the commission on the boundary between British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, instructing it to survey those boundaries and to report to the parliament of Canada and to the legislature of the province of British Columbia.
The commission comprised the surveyor general of Canada, as usual, and the surveyor general of British Columbia. The commission undertook the survey of the boundary in 1945 and pursued the work from 1945 to 1959. Six hundred and twenty-two miles of boundary were surveyed; there are 39 miles more to survey at the western extremity. Those 39 miles lie on extremely difficult glacial terrain which holds no immediate interest for the mining industry in particular.
When the work was completed, the commission wrote its report, dated February 15, 1966. This report included a map showing the location of the surveyed boundaries and the monuments placed on the ground for site identification. This document was tabled in the House of Commons on December 14, 1966.
It may perhaps be asked-I see that some hon. members are absent, fortunately


-under what constitutional authority the federal government engaged in boundary surveying. The answer to that will be found in the British North America Act of 1871. Indeed, the act provides that the parliament of Canada may from time to time, with the consent of the legislature of any province, increase, diminish, or otherwise alter the limits of such province, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed to by the said legislature, i.e., with the consent of provincial authorities.
By applying these provisions now, we can substitute the line of monuments on the ground for the abstract mathematical concept of the sixtieth parallel of north latitude,, mentioned in particular in the Imperial Act of 1866.
The British Columbia legislature passed an act entitled: An Act of Consent respecting the Adoption of the British Columbia-Yukon-Northwest Territories Boundary, which was sanctioned on March 23, 1967. Therefore, the conditions imposed by the British North America Act of 1871 have been fully complied with, and there only remains for the house to pass, if it will, the bill introduced tonight.

When one examines the budget, one finds that it clearly reflects the situation in Canada at present. The federal government is now increasing the tax on tobacco and spirits, apart from imposing a special surtax on the basic personal income tax.
Hardly a year ago, the Quebec government did exactly the same thing. Within a year, as a matter of fact, ten of eleven months later, the federal government increases the tax on spirits and cigarettes. In addition, it increases the personal income tax, which means that we, Canadian citizens, are the only ones in the world to have two governments entitled to levy taxes from us.
December 8, 1967

In the last two years, the Quebec government has increased the sales tax by 2 per cent; the federal government has increased it by 1 per cent. The Quebec government increased the personal income tax; the government in Ottawa did the same. The Quebec government increased the tax on certain goods, and so did Ottawa. We are the only people in the world who accept and tolerate that two different governments should have the right to tax us, very often, for the same purposes.
Our money is being grabbed from both sides. When two governments levy taxes, this entails expenditures that could be avoided if one government only managed our affairs. Let me give you a few examples, Mr. Speaker.
The federal government pays family allowances to children under 16 years of age; so does the Quebec government. Has anyone considered for a moment that this means that civil servants in Ottawa make a survey of all the children under 16, others keep the records up to date, prepare the family allowance cheques, stamp and mail them?
All this is happening in Ottawa, while other civil servants in Quebec do exactly the same thing in respect to family allowance cheques for children in Quebec. This duplicates the expenditures, since both Ottawa and Quebec have to set up a classification system, with a list of names of all children with respect to family allowances. Both governments have to have their own personnel____
which makes it twice as large-to send out family allowance cheques. In addition, two series of cheques and envelopes have to be used; Ottawa pays the postage once, and Quebec a second time. For postage costs only, the federal government expenditure for family allowances amounts to $2.2 million per year. Then, postage has to be paid again in Quebec to mail other family allowance cheques concerning the same children.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, how stupid it is to have a system under which citizens are governed by two separate administrations both doing the same thing at twice the cost, when one expense would be sufficient, just to send out family allowance cheques? Would it not be better to have only one administrative service, using only one envelope for both cheques?
The same thing goes for the Department of National Revenue.

With pleasure, Mr. Chairman. I have indicated that this problem deserved consideration and I am happy to be reminded of this by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Forest) at this stage.
I think that if proceedings in separation have been started in the provincial courts with subsidiary or corollary relief concerning the custody of the children, alimony, etc., and that, later, a petition for divorce is introduced and accepted by the courts, it seems to me that when a divorce decree becomes absolute, there does not seem to be any doubt that a divorce having occurred, judicial separation ceases to exist and, as a result, the corollary relief ordered under the separation decree would also cease to exist. In other words, and I base this on the jurisprudence of our courts, when a divorce decree occurs, the bond is broken and there is no longer any question of separation of bed and board because, under the law, there is no longer any marriage.
Therefore, the effects resulting from a judicial separation no longer exist, as would be the situation if one of the parties died. There is a breach of the marriage bond, there is a breaking off of the cause which resulted in subsidiary effects and, therefore, in such a case, the federal act on divorce would prevail, not because of a precedence of the federal act on the provincial act, but because the decree of divorce, once again, destroys the very bond of marriage and thus destroys the effects which may result from a decree of separation. The conflict would be resolved in that way.
The other hypothesis which might be proposed in theory would be: Could the court which granted a decree of separation amend its decree after the divorce? Certainly not, since the divorce ended the marriage.
This brings me to deal with another question raised the other day by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme) about the conservatory measures which can be taken under the Civil Code and the Code of Civil Procedure now in force in the province of Quebec, and which should be taken before the superior court. [DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
I should like to talk about what I would call the sweet smell of decay which has surrounded a good part of the supposedly entertainment programming of the C.B.C., particularly in some of its most prestigious spots on the prime time. I took the position that the good things it did were quite capable of balancing out the odd utter failure that would happen every so often. In spite of the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond I do not quite see why the public should have to sit back and in a sense allow itself to be hammered over the head by material that is pointless, tasteless, provocative and expensive or have to turn it off after they become sick of writhing as they watch it, knowing that they are paying for it through taxation. Although the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond may equate the sums which go through by the means of advertising into program production to those which come through the public purse, I do know that although you can stop buying the product-you do not have to buy the soap or detergent or whatever it may be-you cannot stop paying taxes. Mr. Chairman, I have been moved to take part in this debate by the remarks of the hon. member for York-Hum-ber. I have never known so many people to be moved by that hon. member's speeches. Let me set straight a fairy story that has been told here during the past two or three hours. It has to do with the suggestion that this house has control over the spending estimates of any department. Where is the hon. member of this house who can remember a time when the estimates of a department have been reduced in this house? I suggest this has never happened in modern history. Surely, this is a fairy story or a myth.
This myth, as described by the hon. member for York Humber, is to the effect that the elective representatives have some control over the government and the C.B.C. As I have mentioned, and as the minister could explain if she were so inclined, the fact of the matter is that the department heads and the president of the C.B.C. decide how much money they need, be it $114 million or more. The estimates then go to the cabinet and to the treasury board. Usually, the treasury board cuts the estimates by perhaps 25 per cent. These department heads and the C.B.C. officials are smart enough to add 30 per cent to their budget needs and they end up better than even.
These estimates then come to the house and are the subject of votes of non-confidence. The rules are such that when the estimates are before the house hon. members can talk about the lumber industry in British Columbia, the fishing and coal industries in the maritimes or anything else they wish. The fact of the matter is that no one talks about the estimates. Finally a member, like that gentleman who is now a feature writer, Mr. Douglas Fisher, moves that the estimates be reduced from $114 million, or whatever they might be, to $1. That usually is the final vote. At no time does it seem that anyone ever questions why the C.B.C. or any other department needs the money it has requested. This whole thing is nothing more than a myth or an exercise.

About the fall of 1964 the committee on parliamentary procedure made a report. At about that time the Prime Minister said in this house he thought it would be a very good idea if departmental estimates were taken out of the house and put into committee. He said that this would give the backbencher and parliamentary committees a certain sense of representative power. He said they could examine these departmental estimates, make recommendations and determine the amounts of money to be made available.
This all sounded very reasonable, because members of parliament could then question the officials of the department as to their money needs. They could also reduce the amounts available to the civil service to carry out these many ventures. If members of parliament had these powers, I am sure a great deal of attention would be paid to what the members had to say. When the amended rules were presented it was obvious that the estimates of the departments may be referred to committees for examination only. The committees can not determine the amount of estimates nor even make recommendations that are likely to be accepted. That is the fact in our parliamentary system.
These criticisms have been placed on the record for the past 25, 30 or 40 years, and I refer to the fact that this house has absolutely no control over departmental spending. We are now asked to approve five year budgeting.
* (9:30 p.m.)
I can see nothing at all wrong with that. In fact, most businesses and enterprises today find it necessary, in order to conduct a good endeavour, to plan five years ahead. I can see nothing wrong with the Department of Finance doing the same thing. In fact, we should be giving very serious attention to making plans over a longer period, say between three and five years, so that business in this nation will know what it is facing, agriculture will know what it is facing and the C.B.C. will know what it is facing. Let us forget this myth, this fairy story about parliamentary control over spending.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order with respect to the ruling because I think it might create a serious precedent. The precedent which will apparently be created is

that no member of the house, whether English or French speaking, will be permitted to move an amendment in committee unless he submits it in writing in both languages. In my opinion this is contrary to the rules, practices and precedents of the house. It has been a matter of courtesy for members to prepare four or five copies of any amendment they intend to propose, one for each party. But there is no requirement that this be done. It is merely required that the amendment be handed to the chairman in writing in either official language, not in both languages. The reason I am apprehensive about this ruling is that if it is allowed to stand, hon. members who are not capable of preparing an amendment in both languages will be prevented from having it accepted by the Chair or presented to the committee.
No member of the committee has the right to demand that an amendment be presented to him in writing in one particular language. All he has the right to demand is that the amendment be read by the Chair, and when it is read by the Chair it is translated simultaneously into the other language. I have no objection to, and I think it is a good practice for, hon. members to present their amendments in writing in both languages for the sake of convenience. However, we now find ourselves in a situation where apparently a precedent is to be set that unless an amendment is presented to the chairman in writing in both languages it will not be accepted or presented to the committee. This will set a precedent for future procedure on amendments.

January 30, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
I say that these words are so vague that they would not enable one to come to a fair conclusion. Therefore I believe the commission would have an impossible task in endeavouring to reach its decision on the objectives. This would seem to be a situation where we have nothing against nothing, when we attempt to reach a decision under subclause (h). In that case I can hardly see how the decision could be based on the objectives of the national broadcasting system, until these are spelled out. Obviously they will have to be spelled out in detail by the national broadcasting system. Therefore the broadcasting system will go before the board and say that in conformity with their general approach to a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment they feel that a certain situation must apply. If we should find that this is part of our objective and that this is the way it is applied, how could others hold a contrary view because they reached their decision under the umbrella of subclauses (d) and (g)?
Subclauses (d) and (g) were designed to express as clearly as possible what the objectives are, but they certainly were never set up to spell out particular cases or to give anyone the ability to say what is meant in a particular case. Surely subclauses (d) and (g) are very much like a statute which would say that the public broadcasting system may enact regulations, which regulations would spell out exactly what is meant. So in this case we have the ability of the national broadcasting service to spell out by regulation the case it is trying to put before the commission. I believe it would be an impossible and unfair task for the commission to attempt to make anything out of subclauses (d) and (g) in respect of a specific case, if the broadcasting system claimed that it was in the national interest.

It would permit the national broadcasting service to declare its own objectives specifically, and therefore hamper any independent decision by the commission.

Mr. Chairman, as regards clause 40, I have no objection to the principle here, but I have as regards the wording.
February 5, 1968

It states that the corporation "is an agent of Her Majesty". Subclauses (1) and (2) provide the following:
The Corporation may, on behalf of Her Majesty, enter into contracts in the name of Her Majesty or in the name of the Corporation.
Subclause (3) states the following:
Property acquired by the Corporation is the property of Her Majesty-
How is it that the Canadian people pay taxes and that all that will be the property of Her Majesty? That is what is written here:
Property acquired by the Corporation is the property of Her Majesty and title thereto may be vested in the name of Her Majesty or in the name of the Corporation.
Subclause (4) reads as follows:
Actions, suits or other legal proceedings in respect of any right or obligation acquired or incurred by the Corporation on behalf of Her Majesty, whether in its name or in the name of Her Majesty-

Property acquired by the Corporation-
All that is acquired by the corporation is so acquired through our taxes and, in no case, in the name of Her Majesty. I cannot accept that.
I heard this afternoon extracts of the federal-provincial conference where objection was taken to similar expressions. I wonder if it would not be possible instead to say that the whole thing belongs to the Canadian people and not to Her Majesty. I am completely against that.

It is not always pleasant, not always satisfactory, to Canadians to see their income tax being raised. But I feel that, in the present system, the way we raise taxes is patently unjust. The little man is still going to pay for everything. There is no end to the little man's taxes. He is taxed on all sorts of things: on production and on consumer buying. He is also taxed by the federal and provincial governments, the municipalities and the school boards, to such an extent that he is left with nothing to live on.
Our citizens find it very hard to make a living, especially the poor and those belonging to the middle class. The middle class is now in the process of disappearing, because it is overtaxed. Here in this house, we are unable to administer. We cannot do anything

without raising taxes and the rates of interest to financiers.
When the money lords raise their rates, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) does not blame them. One would think that he is pleased when the financiers come and raise their rates on capital, stocks and debentures. Everywhere, this is accepted with open arms.
Bonds are renewed, thus increasing capitalization from $500 to $700 million or any other amount, each time raising the interest rate. Now, those gentlemen have done nothing to receive much more than their capital, while the individual has to work and reduce his own capital. The person who lends his capital sees his income and his capital increase as a result of various increases, including interest rates.
I have here, Mr. Chairman, a table which could make the minister and the hon. members understand.
It is a comparative table for the years 1944 to 1967.
The gross national product amounted to some $11,400 million in 1944, while it reached $62 billion in 1967.
Consumption and expenditures amounted to only $10,120 million in 1944, compared to $40 billion in 1967.
During the same period, capitalization and profits increased from $1,280 million to $22 billion. This means, therefore, that capitalization and profits have increased 17-fold from 1944 to 1967, while the gross national product increased five-fold and consumption and expenditures, four-fold.

The Seaboard Finance Company of Canada is an Ontario incorporated company which seeks federal incorporation under the Small Loans Act. I believe it already is a known fact that this company engages in business throughout Canada under its provincial charter. So, should this company be granted federal incorporation, the only benefit that would accrue to it would be that it would have a little greater status in the community because the federal parliament had placed its hand upon it stating that it is free to go out in the business world to conduct the business of small loans.
The Seaboard Finance Company of Canada is a totally owned subsidiary of a large foreign investment company. The Prime Minister has stated that it is his belief and wish that Canadian industry and financial institutions should come progressively more and more under the jurisdiction of Canadian citizens. We believe this to be a good precedent. I should like to support the Prime Minister by saying that these companies which control large blocks of shares in our country should be under Canadian ownership and therefore responsive more to the needs of Canada and less to the needs and influences of a foreign country.
We are reluctant therefore to grant our blessing to this company, that it should go out into the world to conduct this business. Moneylenders have been with us since the beginning of time I presume. They are mentioned in the Bible. In the old days the moneylenders went into the temples and the high priests drove them with whips out of the temple. I do not propose that the moneylenders in this day and age should be whipped, but they certainly do not contribute to the well-being of our country when they charge usurious rates of interest to the people who are placed in the predicament of having to come into their clutches.
Under the Small Loans Act the Canadian people have borrowed approximately $900 million in order to acquire for themselves the

things they need to carry on the business of living in Canada today. When we consider that the rate charged under the Small Loans Act sometimes is as high as 24 per cent we realize that a great deal of money which could otherwise be directed toward the production of more consumer goods is being siphoned off in the form of interest. If a greater percentage of this money which is paid out in the form of interest was retained as spending power in the hands of the consumers, I am sure more employment would be created. We would have a better standard of living and the whole economy of the nation would be improved if this money which is now being paid out in the form of usurious interest were left in the hands of the spender.

The capital investment
required and the vast technical knowledge and special equipment needed in farming make it virtually impossible these days for farmers to change their fields of endeavour. If they did, in most instances the result would be economic ruin. Some farmers who financed their farms knew that it would take at least a generation to pay off the debt. That was done deliberately. Therefore, to speak of phasing out now is absolute nonsense.
Sixth, I wish to speak of long-range plans. To create economic units, as the government has suggested should be done, requires a tremendous amount of capital, absolute business management and indispensable long-range planning. By its bungling the government has caused tremendous damage. Its long-range policies do well to last the test of one year.

March 1, 1968
Supply-Agriculture
As prime examples of my contention I cite the three different dairy policies we have had in three years and the government's on again, off again, turkey import quotas.
Seventh, the confusion in the dairy industry would be comic if it were not so tragic. Dairy farmers in Ontario today are placed in an untenable position. Federal policy is explicitly directed toward shutting down small producers and forcing large units to produce greater volumes more efficiently. At the same time a provincial policy places limited quotas on producers, thus making expansion into larger production units almost impossible. Who says farmers never had it so good? Through the Department of Agriculture the government spends the taxpayers' money to expand tobacco production; through the Department of National Health and Welfare it spends the taxpayers' money to curtail the domestic consumption of tobacco.
Never had it so good? Our young people and our old people are leaving the land by the thousands. Our best cattle are being dispersed all over the world. Our best farm land is being covered with concrete and buildings. Our domestic markets are fast shrinking under the constant pressure of cheap imports. Canadian agriculture, once great and world admired, has been reduced to a state of clawing frantically for survival.
The government constantly whines when it is confronted with these facts. It asks, "What did you do when you were in power? Where were your policies?" When we were in office our policy was designed to keep farmers on the farms if they wanted to stay.

However I would not want to niggle about division of responsibility, because the main problem in Canada now in connection with pollution control is division of responsibility. There are so many commissions, organizations and levels of government involved that from the action point of view we have almost reached an impasse.

I believe these reports are greatly exaggerated, and that the situation is not as disturbed as it has been made out to be.
However, the developments of the last few days have resulted in a marked increase in the short term rates of interest in the so-called Euro-dollar market. These rates have 27053-454
risen to very high levels. In view of the already high level of short term rates of interest in Canada it has been thought desirable to protect the Canadian interest rate structure from the effect of these short term rates in the Euro-dollar market as far as we can.
The governor of the Bank of Canada has this morning, by agreement with me requested the banks and other financial intermediaries for the time being not to facilitate swapped deposit transactions, which constitute the main link between the Canadian short term interest rate structure and the rate prevailing in the Euro-dollar market.
I wish therefore to request Canadian investors for the time being to refrain from entering into or renewing swapped deposit transactions through any intermediary, Canadian or non-Canadian. By way of explanation I should add that swapped deposits are made with Canadian funds which are converted into a foreign currency, usually U.S. dollars, and placed on term deposit with a bank or other intermediary, with the intermediary undertaking through a forward contract to convert them back into Canadian dollars at maturity.

Mr. Speaker, in June, 1956, on a Thursday afternoon at 5.15, which has become a notable period in Canada's history, I raised a point of order on the subject of whether or not the Chairman of Committees should make a ruling which was not based on precedents established by the Speaker or not founded on decisions that have been arrived at by the Speaker. I argued the point, supported strongly by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that there was a danger in having a body of rules established in committee of the whole, because we noted that from time to time the person who presides in committee of the whole is shifted. He is not always the Deputy Speaker. My point then, and I had quite a number of references to give, was that when the Chairman of Committees has no precedent to guide him,

established by the Speaker himself, the matter should be held in abeyance and the decision should be made by the Speaker rather than by the Chairman. It would avoid these embarrassing and awkward situations where a chairman is overruled by the Speaker.

There are 28 treatment institutions strategically located throughout the Northwest Territories. All will continue to be operated throughout the coming year and a number of health centres, health stations and dispensers will also continue to provide services. After the recent accelerated expansion of medical and public health services, including the introduction of total hospital insurance coverage and the
March 7, 19G8

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion development of an exclusively northern region of medical services, some levelling off in the rate of expansion now seems reasonable, especially since the major causes of the high rates of disease and death are not related either to lack of public health effort or to lack of treatment facilities.
Sixty per cent of the population of the Northwest Territories is comprised of Indians and Eskimos whose mode of living belongs to a more primitive age than that of the populations of the southern provinces. The high birth rates and the high proportion of young people in the population increases problems of child care in the homes. Poverty, the low level of socio-economic development, lack of education in the older age groups, the severe climate, inadequate housing and overcrowding of the limited space a family can afford to heat, all play a significant role as causes of pneumonia, accidents and diseases of infancy.
During the year 1966 the chief causes of death in the Northwest Territories were pneumonia, 22.3 per cent, injuries and violence, 18.9 per cent and malformations and diseases associated with infancy, 17.9 per cent. During the past few years great strides have been made toward the improvement of living conditions. Whole settlements have been rebuilt. Special attention has been paid to
public health engineering problems affecting the provision of potable water at all seasons, and safe, sanitary disposal of sewage.
In 1956 the infant mortality rate for Eskimos was 240 per 1,000 live births. By 1966 this had fallen to 100, for Eskimos. For all groups the infant mortality rate was 140 in 1956 and by 1966 it had fallen to below 80. Measures such as a full program of immunization and health education by public health nurses and trained community health workers are carried on in greater intensity in northern communities than in any other part of Canada. Improved diagnostic programs are turning up more cases of tuberculosis; but this is considered to be the result of increased effectiveness rather than lack of good health practices. Improved housing and nutrition will complement the role of the health department.
In the current year a total of $7,880,000 is being directed to northern health services. This is an increase of 14 per cent over the corresponding sum of $6,920,000 for the year 1966-67. Such a rate of growth repeated year after year would be abnormal and the intention for the year 1968-69 is to hold the line at essentially the current year's level and allocate $7,900,000 to northern health services.

Mr. Chairman, I have two or three brief comments on this item and also one proposal. I think the film board performs a very useful and rather underrated service to Canada. I am told that at least 16 million people in Canada see one production or another of the film board every year and that 30 million people in other countries see productions of the National Film Board. The quality of the N.F.B. productions is indicated by the fact that over recent years more than 600 international awards have been won by the National Film Board for its work.
The work of the board is not confined simply to the production of films. Some of its employees are working on improvements in technical equipment which may be very useful. The board also plays a useful role in helping various departments of government by illustrating their efforts. In this regard I think the film board is to be commended.
The proposal I want to make and draw particularly to the attention of the Secretary of State, if I may, concerns what seems to me to be an urgent need for some action at the federal level to preserve historic Canadian film. Two or three archive organizations in this country are trying to do something along that line but I believe that they are not receiving sufficient financial support from the Canadian public. The film that the Canadian Film Institute is trying to preserve is irreplaceable. It is old film having to do with the earliest beginnings of the Canadian film industry. It is a sad fact to relate that last year a million feet of this historic film was burned because it was insecurely stored. In concluding my remarks I take the opportunity to direct the attention of the Secretary of State to this problem and to urge her to do what she can to draw together those connec-ed with film archives to see whether or not they can work out with federal aid a program that will really protect historic Canadian film.

After two days he went back to the original wholesaler and said he would accept the first offer, but this wholesaler already said that he could not offer the producer any more. Then later, Mr. Chairman, we tried to sell our fruit direct to the co-operatives on the prairies or to small country stores. But do you know what the brokers and wholesalers did? I wish him well in all he undertakes in this direction.

The house will, I am sure, welcome the decisions announced yesterday in Washington by the governors of the central banks contributing to the gold pool. The governor of the Bank of Canada announced that as part of this arrangement the reciprocal credit facility between the Bank of Canada and the federal reserve system has been increased from U.S. $750 million to U.S. $1,000 million.
